rationale: Start with a broad gradient to map the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test selectivity around the sole unresolved pair. The current elution window is comfortably below 10 minutes, so improving that pair could reach the maximum CRF.

The central peak pattern suggests an elution-order crossing between 40 and 50 C; moving to 55 C may separate the crossing pair further. A slightly shallower gradient should help protect resolution of the neighboring pair while keeping the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Keep the promising 55 C selectivity and make the gradient slightly shallower to lift the critical pair above R = 1.5. The last peak at 8.60 minutes leaves some room for the added retention without incurring a time penalty.

At 55 C, lengthening the gradient reduced the critical pair’s resolution, so shorten it to 12 minutes to test the favorable direction. This may lift that pair above 1.5 while retaining adequate neighboring separation and reducing elution time.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF; now test a shorter gradient to seek a faster fully resolved method. Monitor the narrowly resolved central pairs, retaining injection 5 as the benchmark if either falls below 1.5.

Return to the successful 12-minute gradient duration and test a higher starting organic fraction as an alternative way to shorten retention. This probes whether shifting the gradient window can preserve both critical separations better than shortening the gradient did.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with the faster 10-minute gradient, since the high-temperature region trades resolution between two critical pairs. This tests a distinct route to a shorter fully resolved method while preserving injection 5 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a substantially faster gradient at the highest temperature to explore whether the central peaks separate again after an elution-order crossing. This is an exploratory speed test; injection 5 remains the fully resolved, maximum-CRF benchmark.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves selectivity among the central peaks in the fast 60 C method. Injection 5 already achieves maximum CRF, so this explores a substantially shorter alternative without replacing that benchmark.

Explore intermediate-low temperature selectivity with a shorter gradient, since the fast 60 C methods leave two central pairs unresolved. This samples a different selectivity region while retaining injection 5 as the maximum-score method.

Refine injection 7 by slightly reducing the gradient slope, aiming to raise its R = 1.29 pair above 1.5 while preserving the other critical pair. This tests a nearby alternative to the maximum-score method with a higher starting organic fraction.

Reduce the endpoint by one more grid step to improve the pair that reached R = 1.47 in injection 12. The other critical pair has a small margin, and the last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Shift the gradient window upward at the start while further reducing its slope, following the selectivity improvement from injections 12–13. This tests whether both critical pairs can gain resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 5 remains the fastest maximum-score method.

Test the effect of one temperature step above injection 3 while keeping its gradient fixed. This will clarify whether 60 C can improve the limiting pair without sacrificing its neighboring separation, with ample room below the 10-minute time threshold.

Higher starting organic fractions have improved the later critical pair at 55 C but weakened its neighbor; lowering to 50 C may compensate for that trade-off. Test this shifted window for a faster fully resolved alternative while retaining injection 5 as the benchmark.

Use a shallower gradient to recover the neighboring pair that limited injection 14, whose other critical pair had R = 1.75. This seeks a maximum-score method with more resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test whether shortening the 40 C gradient improves its limiting central separation, as shortening did at 55 C. This explores a faster alternative near the strong initial result while retaining injection 5 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Refine the fastest maximum-score method with a slightly shallower gradient to test whether its two critical separations can be better balanced. This intermediate slope lies between injections 5 and 3 and should keep the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Use a slope between those of injections 12 and 13 to seek the fastest fully resolved method in this gradient window. The endpoint remains above the organic fraction at which the last peak previously eluted, limiting the risk of prolonged retention during the hold.

Preserve injection 5’s successful gradient slope and temperature while ending the programmed ramp two minutes earlier. All peaks previously eluted before this new ramp endpoint reaches the outlet, so this should retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Shorten the programmed ramp again while preserving the successful slope of injections 5 and 21. Its endpoint reaches the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after the observed last peak at 7.60 minutes, so the separation should retain maximum CRF.

Test an earlier transition to the final hold while preserving the successful slope through all critical pairs. The last peak may elute later during the hold, so this tests whether a shorter ramp and lower final organic fraction can retain maximum CRF without exceeding 10 minutes.

Test a modest slope increase from injection 21 to seek a last peak earlier than 7.60 minutes. This is a finer speed challenge than injection 6, with the central R = 1.59 pair expected to set the limit; retain injection 22 if resolution falls below 1.5.

Use the final injection to refine the fully resolved method from injection 13, lowering its endpoint one step to improve the neighboring critical separation while monitoring the later pair. This should remain below 10 minutes; injections 5, 21, and 22 remain the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF methods.
